title: Loss Aversion

scenes.text: Losing ₹100 feels *worse* than finding ₹100 feels good
scenes.vo: Losing 100 rupees feels way worse than finding 100 rupees feels good. Why?

scenes.text: Your brain treats losing as about *2×* bigger
scenes.vo: Scientists found that for your brain, losing something hits about twice as hard as winning the same thing.

scenes.text:
Coin toss:
Heads, win ₹100
Tails, lose ₹100
scenes.vo: Imagine a coin toss. Heads, you win 100 rupees. Tails, you lose 100. Would you play?
Most people say no. Losing 100 feels worse than winning 100 feels good.
This is called loss aversion. Aversion just means you really, really don't like something.
It's why free trials work. Once you have something, cancelling feels like losing it. And it's why you panic when your game streak is about to break.

scenes.text: Ask: am I keeping this because I *like* it, or because I hate losing it?
scenes.vo: So ask yourself: am I keeping this because I actually like it, or just because I hate losing it?

caption:
Your brain hates losing about twice as much as it loves winning. 📉 That's loss aversion, and it's the reason that streak notification works on you.

What's a streak you refuse to break? 🔥👇
source: Kahneman, D. & Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect Theory. Econometrica, 47(2).
